item.title: Dynamic Configuration Settings
item.description:
Source: https://patroni.readthedocs.io/en/latest/dynamic_configuration.html

Dynamic configuration is stored in the DCS (Distributed Configuration Store) and applied on all cluster nodes.

Change dynamic configuration with patronictl_edit_config or the Patroni REST API.

  • loop_wait: the number of seconds the loop will sleep. Default value: 10, minimum possible value: 1
  • ttl: leader lock TTL, in seconds. This is the interval before automatic failover can start. Default: 30. Minimum: 20.
  • retry_timeout: timeout for DCS and PostgreSQL operation retries (in seconds). DCS or network issues shorter than this will not cause Patroni to demote the leader. Default value: 10, minimum possible value: 3
Warning

when changing values of loop_wait, retry_timeout, or ttl you have to follow the rule:

loop_wait + 2 * retry_timeout <= ttl

item.title: Introduction
item.description:
Source: https://patroni.readthedocs.io/en/latest/README.html

Patroni is a Python template for high availability (HA) PostgreSQL solutions. It started as a fork of Governor, a Compose project, and adds many features.

For additional background info, see:

  • PostgreSQL HA with Kubernetes and Patroni, talk by Josh Berkus at KubeCon 2016 (video)
  • Feb. 2016 Zalando Tech blog post

Development Status

Patroni is in active development and accepts contributions. See Contributing for details.

See release information for new releases.

item.title: YAML Configuration Settings
item.description:
Source: https://patroni.readthedocs.io/en/latest/yaml_configuration.html

Global/Universal

  • thread_pool_size: thread pool size for asynchronous tasks and REST API communication with other members during leader races or failsafe checks. Minimum: 5. Default: 5.
  • thread_stack_size: stack size for Patroni threads. Use a multiple of 64kB. Minimum: 64kB. Patroni default: 512kB.
  • name: the name of the host. Must be unique for the cluster. The value __patroni_strict_sync_replica_placeholder__ is reserved for internal use by Patroni and cannot be used as a node name.
  • namespace: path within the configuration store where Patroni will keep information about the cluster. Default value: “/service”
  • scope: cluster name

item.title: Environment Configuration Settings
item.description:
Source: https://patroni.readthedocs.io/en/latest/ENVIRONMENT.html

System environment variables can override some Patroni configuration file parameters. This page lists all supported variables. Environment values always take precedence over file values.

Global/Universal

  • PATRONI_CONFIGURATION: sets the complete Patroni configuration through PATRONI_CONFIGURATION. Patroni then ignores all other environment variables.
  • PATRONI_THREAD_POOL_SIZE: thread pool size for asynchronous tasks and REST API communication with other members during leader races or failsafe checks. Minimum: 5. Default: 5.
  • PATRONI_THREAD_STACK_SIZE: stack size for Patroni threads. Use a multiple of 64kB. Minimum: 64kB. Patroni default: 512kB.
  • PATRONI_NAME: name of the node where the current instance of Patroni is running. Must be unique for the cluster. The value __patroni_strict_sync_replica_placeholder__ is reserved for internal use by Patroni and cannot be used as a node name.
  • PATRONI_NAMESPACE: path within the configuration store where Patroni will keep information about the cluster. Default value: “/service”
  • PATRONI_SCOPE: cluster name
  • PG_MALLOC_ARENA_MAX: custom value for MALLOC_ARENA_MAX environment variable for postmaster process. If not set, postmaster will inherit MALLOC_ARENA_MAX value.

Log

  • PATRONI_LOG_TYPE: sets the format of logs. Can be either plain or json. To use json format, you must have the jsonlogger installed. The default value is plain.
  • PATRONI_LOG_LEVEL: sets the general logging level. Default value is INFO (see the docs for Python logging)
  • PATRONI_LOG_TRACEBACK_LEVEL: sets the level where tracebacks will be visible. Default value is ERROR. Set it to DEBUG if you want to see tracebacks only if you enable PATRONI_LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG.
  • PATRONI_LOG_FORMAT: log format. For plain logs, use a string. For json, use a string or a list of LogRecord attributes. In lists, use field names without %( and ). To rename a field, use a dictionary with the original field as key and the output name as value. Default: %(asctime)s %(levelname)s: %(message)s.
  • PATRONI_LOG_DATEFORMAT: sets the datetime formatting string. (see the formatTime() documentation)
  • PATRONI_LOG_STATIC_FIELDS: add additional fields to the log. This option is only available when the log type is set to json. Example PATRONI_LOG_STATIC_FIELDS="{app: patroni}"
  • PATRONI_LOG_MAX_QUEUE_SIZE: maximum internal log queue size. Patroni writes records to an in-memory queue. A separate thread reads them and writes to stderr or a file. The default 1000 records retain approximately 1h20m of logs.
  • PATRONI_LOG_DIR: application log directory. It must exist and be writable by the Patroni user. By default, Patroni retains four 25MB files. Adjust retention with PATRONI_LOG_FILE_NUM and PATRONI_LOG_FILE_SIZE.
  • PATRONI_LOG_MODE: Permissions for log files (for example, 0644). If not specified, permissions will be set based on the current umask value.
  • PATRONI_LOG_FILE_NUM: The number of application logs to retain.
  • PATRONI_LOG_FILE_SIZE: Size of patroni.log file (in bytes) that triggers a log rolling.
  • PATRONI_LOG_LOGGERS: Redefine logging level per python module. Example PATRONI_LOG_LOGGERS="{patroni.postmaster: WARNING, urllib3: DEBUG}"
  • PATRONI_LOG_DEDUPLICATE_HEARTBEAT_LOGS: suppresses consecutive identical heartbeat messages when true. Default: false.
Warning

HA loop timing helps diagnose failovers caused by exhausted resources and similar problems. With PATRONI_LOG_DEDUPLICATE_HEARTBEAT_LOGS set to true, loop execution produces no log unless the leader changes. These diagnostics are then unavailable in the logs.

item.title: Patroni configuration
item.description:
Source: https://patroni.readthedocs.io/en/latest/patroni_configuration.html

There are 3 types of Patroni configuration:

  • Global dynamic configuration.
    These options are stored in the DCS (Distributed Configuration Store) and apply to all nodes. Change them at any time with patronictl_edit_config or the REST API. Changes outside startup configuration apply asynchronously on each node’s next wake-up cycle, followed by a reload. Changed PostgreSQL parameters with postmaster context require a restart. Patroni sets pending_restart in members.data JSON for these nodes. Node status also shows "restart_pending": true.

  • Local configuration file (patroni.yml).
    Local options override dynamic configuration. To reload patroni.yml without restarting Patroni, send SIGHUP, send POST /reload, or run patronictl_reload. Local configuration can be one YAML file or a directory. Patroni loads all YAML files in a directory in sorted order. If several files define a key, the last file takes precedence.

  • Environment configuration.
    Environment variables can set or override some local parameters. Use them in dynamic environments where some values are unknown in advance. For example, the external IP address may be unknown inside docker.

item.title: Patroni REST API
item.description:
Source: https://patroni.readthedocs.io/en/latest/rest_api.html

Patroni uses its REST API during leader races. patronictl uses it for failovers, switchovers, reinitialization, restarts, and reloads. HAProxy and other load balancers use it for HTTP health checks. Monitoring systems can also use it. This page lists the available endpoints.

Health check endpoints

Health check GET requests return an HTTP status code and a JSON document with node status. Use HEAD or OPTIONS instead of GET if you do not need JSON.

item.title: patronictl
item.description:
Source: https://patroni.readthedocs.io/en/latest/patronictl.html

The patronictl command-line interface communicates with the Patroni REST API and the DCS. Use it for cluster operations, interactively or in scripts.

Configuration

patronictl uses 3 sections of the configuration:

  • ctl: REST API authentication and server identity verification. See ctl settings.
  • restapi: fallback settings when ctl does not supply REST API authentication or server verification. patronictl uses restapi.authentication if ctl.authentication is absent, and restapi.cafile if ctl.cacert is absent. See REST API settings.
  • DCS, such as etcd: DCS connection and authentication settings.

Supply these options through environment variables or a configuration file. See the corresponding sections in Environment Configuration Settings and YAML Configuration Settings.

item.title: Replica imaging and bootstrap
item.description:
Source: https://patroni.readthedocs.io/en/latest/replica_bootstrap.html

Patroni supports custom replica creation and custom bootstrap for a new, empty cluster. These are separate operations. Patroni creates replicas only when the cluster has an initialize key in the DCS. Without that key, only the first node to acquire the initialize lock runs bootstrap.

Bootstrap

By default, Patroni initializes new clusters with PostgreSQL initdb. Some operations, such as copying an existing cluster, require a custom bootstrap method. Patroni can run a user-defined script and supply the cluster name and data directory. Configure this in the bootstrap section:

item.title: Replication modes
item.description:
Source: https://patroni.readthedocs.io/en/latest/replication_modes.html

Patroni uses PostgreSQL streaming replication. See the Postgres documentation. Patroni configures asynchronous replication by default. Select a replication design for your business requirements. Compare asynchronous replication, synchronous replication, and other HA solutions before you select one.

Asynchronous mode durability

Asynchronous mode permits some committed transaction loss to maintain availability. If the primary fails or becomes unavailable, Patroni automatically promotes a sufficiently healthy standby. Transactions absent from that standby remain on a forked timeline on the old primary. They are effectively unrecoverable1.

item.title: Standby cluster
item.description:
Source: https://patroni.readthedocs.io/en/latest/standby_cluster.html

Patroni supports cascading replication to a remote datacenter or region through the standby cluster feature. A standby cluster has:

  • A standby leader, which behaves like a regular cluster leader but replicates from a remote node.
  • Cascade replicas, which replicate from the standby leader.

The standby leader holds and updates a leader lock in the DCS. If the lock expires, the cascade replicas elect another leader from the standbys.

item.title: Watchdog support
item.description:
Source: https://patroni.readthedocs.io/en/latest/watchdog.html

Multiple PostgreSQL primaries can lose transactions because their timelines diverge. This is called split-brain. Patroni must prevent PostgreSQL from accepting transaction commits after the leader key expires in the DCS. Normally, Patroni stops PostgreSQL if the leader lock update fails for any reason. This protection can fail for these reasons:

  • Patroni crashes because of a bug, insufficient memory, or an accidental kill by a system administrator.
  • PostgreSQL shutdown takes too long.
  • System load, a VM pause by the hypervisor, or other infrastructure problems prevent Patroni from running.

Patroni supports watchdog devices to guarantee correct behavior under these conditions. A software or hardware watchdog resets the whole system if it receives no keepalive heartbeat within a specified time. This adds protection if the usual Patroni split-brain controls fail.

item.title: Pause/Resume mode for the cluster
item.description:
Source: https://patroni.readthedocs.io/en/latest/pause.html

The goal

Patroni sometimes needs to suspend cluster management while it retains cluster state in the DCS. Examples include major version upgrades and corruption recovery. During these operations, nodes often start and stop for reasons that Patroni does not know. Temporary promotions can also violate the assumption that only one primary runs. Pause mode lets Patroni detach from the running cluster, like maintenance mode in Pacemaker.

item.title: DCS Failsafe Mode
item.description:
Source: https://patroni.readthedocs.io/en/latest/dcs_failsafe_mode.html

The problem

Patroni uses the Distributed Configuration Store (DCS) for leader elections and network partition detection. A node can run Postgres as primary only if it can update the DCS leader lock. If the update fails, Patroni immediately demotes Postgres and starts it read-only. Failure frequency depends on the DCS. It is close to zero with Etcd dedicated to Patroni, but can be higher with the Etcd-backed K8s API.

item.title: Using Patroni with Kubernetes
item.description:
Source: https://patroni.readthedocs.io/en/latest/kubernetes.html

Patroni can store cluster state and the leader key in Kubernetes objects. This lets it run Postgres in Kubernetes without a separate consistency store, such as an extra Etcd deployment. Patroni supports two object types for the leader and configuration keys. Select the type with kubernetes.use_endpoints or the PATRONI_KUBERNETES_USE_ENDPOINTS environment variable.

Use Endpoints

This mode is recommended but disabled by default for compatibility. When enabled, Patroni creates Endpoints and stores cluster configuration and the leader key in their metadata: annotations fields. A leader change updates both the leader annotations and the addresses of the leader pod in one operation. This is safer than ConfigMaps.

item.title: Citus support
item.description:
Source: https://patroni.readthedocs.io/en/latest/citus.html

Patroni automates deployment of Multi-Node Citus clusters.

TL;DR

Apply these rules:

  1. Install the Citus PostgreSQL extension on every node. The minimum supported version is 10.0. We recommend at least 11.2 for transparent worker switchovers and restarts.
  2. Use the same cluster name (scope) on all Citus nodes.
  3. Use the same superuser credentials on the coordinator and all workers. Configure pg_hba.conf to permit superuser access between all nodes.
  4. Permit worker access to the coordinator REST API. Use the same credentials. If client certificates are configured, the coordinator must accept worker certificates.
  5. Add this section to patroni.yaml:
citus:
 group: X  # 0 for coordinator and 1, 2, 3, etc for workers
 database: citus  # must be the same on all nodes

Then start Patroni. It performs these operations:

item.title: Convert a Standalone to a Patroni Cluster
item.description:
Source: https://patroni.readthedocs.io/en/latest/existing_data.html

This section describes the process for converting a standalone PostgreSQL instance into a Patroni cluster.

To deploy a Patroni cluster without using a pre-existing PostgreSQL instance, see Running and Configuring instead.

Procedure

The following steps convert an existing Postgres cluster to Patroni management. All nodes must be running. These steps assume you do not intend to change the Postgres configuration during migration.

  1. Create the Postgres users described in the authentication section. In the sample SQL below, replace usernames and passwords for your environment. Skip this step if the required users already exist.

    -- Patroni superuser
-- Replace PATRONI_SUPERUSER_USERNAME and PATRONI_SUPERUSER_PASSWORD accordingly
CREATE USER PATRONI_SUPERUSER_USERNAME WITH SUPERUSER ENCRYPTED PASSWORD 'PATRONI_SUPERUSER_PASSWORD';

-- Patroni replication user
-- Replace PATRONI_REPLICATION_USERNAME and PATRONI_REPLICATION_PASSWORD accordingly
CREATE USER PATRONI_REPLICATION_USERNAME WITH REPLICATION ENCRYPTED PASSWORD 'PATRONI_REPLICATION_PASSWORD';

-- Patroni rewind user, if you intend to enable use_pg_rewind in your Patroni configuration
-- Replace PATRONI_REWIND_USERNAME and PATRONI_REWIND_PASSWORD accordingly
CREATE USER PATRONI_REWIND_USERNAME WITH ENCRYPTED PASSWORD 'PATRONI_REWIND_PASSWORD';
GRANT EXECUTE ON function pg_catalog.pg_ls_dir(text, boolean, boolean) TO PATRONI_REWIND_USERNAME;
GRANT EXECUTE ON function pg_catalog.pg_stat_file(text, boolean) TO PATRONI_REWIND_USERNAME;
GRANT EXECUTE ON function pg_catalog.pg_read_binary_file(text) TO PATRONI_REWIND_USERNAME;
GRANT EXECUTE ON function pg_catalog.pg_read_binary_file(text, bigint, bigint, boolean) TO PATRONI_REWIND_USERNAME;

  2. Complete these steps on each Postgres node. Finish one node before you continue to the next. Start with the primary, then process each standby:

    1. If systemd runs Postgres, disable the Postgres systemd unit. Patroni will manage Postgres startup and shutdown.
    2. Create a Patroni YAML configuration file. You can use Patroni configuration generation and validation tooling.
      • Note (specific for the primary node): If cluster members use replication slots, we recommend enabling use_slots. Configure the existing slots as permanent with slots. When use_slots is enabled, Patroni creates member replication slots and drops slots it does not recognize. Permanent slot configuration preserves your existing slots during migration. See Dynamic Configuration Settings for details.
    3. Start the patroni systemd service. Patroni detects that Postgres is running and starts monitoring it.

  3. Transfer Postgres startup management to Patroni. Restart members with patronictl restart cluster-name member-name. To minimize downtime, you may split this step:

    1. Immediate restart of the standby nodes.
    2. Scheduled restart of the primary node within a maintenance window.

  4. If you configured permanent slots in step 1.2., wait for the Patroni slots to catch up. Their restart_lsn must reach the restart_lsn of the corresponding original slots. Then remove the original slots from slots with patronictl edit-config cluster-name. Patroni can then drop the original slots when they are no longer needed. Use this example query to compare restart_lsn values:

    -- Assume original_slot_for_member_x is the name of the slot in your original
-- cluster for replicating changes to member X, and slot_for_member_x is the
-- slot created by Patroni for that purpose. You need restart_lsn of
-- slot_for_member_x to be >= restart_lsn of original_slot_for_member_x
SELECT slot_name,
 restart_lsn
FROM pg_replication_slots
WHERE slot_name IN (
 'original_slot_for_member_x',
 'slot_for_member_x'
)

item.title: Integration with other tools
item.description:
Source: https://patroni.readthedocs.io/en/latest/tools_integration.html

Patroni can integrate with other tools in your stack. These examples show possible integrations. The list is not complete.

Barman

Patroni provides patroni_barman. This application communicates with pg-backup-api to run Barman operations remotely.

The application has two subcommands: recover and config-switch.

patroni_barman recover

Use the recover subcommand as a custom bootstrap method or replica creation method. See replica_imaging_and_bootstrap for details.

item.title: Security Considerations
item.description:
Source: https://patroni.readthedocs.io/en/latest/security.html

Protect two Patroni cluster interfaces from unauthorized access: the distributed configuration storage (DCS) and the Patroni REST API.

Protecting DCS

Patroni and patronictl store data in the DCS and retrieve data from it.

The DCS contains no sensitive information, but it permits changes to some Patroni/Postgres settings. Protect the DCS first.

Protection depends on the DCS type. See settings for authentication and encryption parameters: tokens, basic authentication, and client certificates.

item.title: HA multi datacenter
item.description:
Source: https://patroni.readthedocs.io/en/latest/ha_multi_dc.html

A PostgreSQL cluster across multiple data centers uses replication for high availability. Replication can be synchronous or asynchronous. See replication modes.

Both modes require these considerations:

  • Postgres can run as primary or standby leader only if it owns and can update the leader key.
  • Use an odd number of etcd, ZooKeeper, or Consul nodes: 3 or 5.

Synchronous Replication

A multi-datacenter cluster needs at least 3 zones to tolerate a zone failure automatically.

item.title: FAQ
item.description:
Source: https://patroni.readthedocs.io/en/latest/faq.html

This section answers common Patroni questions. Each subsection covers a different topic.

For more help or unexpected problems, see chatting and reporting_bugs.

Comparison with other HA solutions

Why does Patroni require a separate cluster of DCS nodes while other solutions like repmgr do not?
There are different ways of implementing HA solutions, each of them with their pros and cons.

Software like repmgr performs communication among the nodes to decide when actions should be taken.

item.title: Release notes
item.description:
Source: https://patroni.readthedocs.io/en/latest/releases.html

Version 4.1.5

Released 2026-08-12

Compatibility improvements

  • Compatibility with PostgreSQL 14.24, 15.19, 16.15, 17.11, 18.6 (Alexander Kukushkin)

    Add the new output_plugin_libraries GUC, which restricts logical decoding output plugins.

Improvements

  • Log REST API connection resets at DEBUG instead of WARNING (Kyle McLaren)

    Ensure the common “client went away mid-write” variants are silenced without affecting the handling of genuine (non-connection) errors.

Bugfixes

  • Fix thread_stack_size validation alignment (Sundong Kim)

    Changed aligned from 65535 to 65536 in the thread_stack_size schema. Previously, patroni --validate-config rejected almost all realistic values, including the daemon default 524288.

  • Allow validation of synchronous_mode to accept 'quorum' and boolean-like strings (Eray Araz)

    patroni --validate-config previously rejected synchronous_mode values such as quorum and the PostgreSQL-style boolean strings that are accepted at runtime.

item.title: Contributing guidelines
item.description:
Source: https://patroni.readthedocs.io/en/latest/contributing_guidelines.html

Chatting

For questions, interactive troubleshooting, or discussion with other users, join #patroni on PostgreSQL Slack.

Reporting bugs

Before you report a bug, reproduce it with the latest Patroni version. Check the Issues Tracker for an existing report.

Running tests

Requirements for running behave tests:

  1. Install PostgreSQL packages, including contrib modules.
  2. Add PostgreSQL binaries to PATH. For example, use PATH=/usr/lib/postgresql/11/bin:\$PATH python -m behave.
  3. For external DCS tests, install the relevant packages, such as Etcd, Consul, or Zookeeper. Run their services on localhost and the default port, with unencrypted, unprotected connections. For Etcd and Consul, the behave suite can start the services if their binaries are in PATH.

item.title: Patroni 4.1.5 Documentation
item.description:
Source: https://patroni.readthedocs.io/en/latest/index.html

Warning

Running Patroni on memory-restricted systems with Python 3.11+

Unexpected behavior can occur with Python 3.11 or newer on systems with strict memory limits. For example, this includes vm.overcommit_memory=2, which is recommended for PostgreSQL. You may observe these symptoms:

  • Patroni appears healthy
  • PostgreSQL continues to run
  • Patroni REST API becomes unresponsive
  • The operating system reports that Patroni is listening on the REST API port
  • Patroni logs look normal; however, following messages may appear once: Exception ignored in thread started by: <object repr() failed>, MemoryError
  • Kernel logs may contain messages such as not enough memory for the allocation

A bug in Python 3.11+ causes this behavior. Under strict memory conditions, a new thread may hang indefinitely if free memory is insufficient.
